title: Greatest common divisor: trial divisors vs Euclid's algorithm
problem_statement: Given non-negative integers a and b, compute gcd(a, b), the largest integer dividing both (with gcd(a, 0) = a and gcd(0, 0) = 0).

input.parameter: n = bit length of max(a, b); both inputs are < 2^n.
input.size_measure: 2n bits at most (standard binary encoding of a and b).

algorithms.name: trial divisors
algorithms.idea: Try d = min(a, b), min(a, b) - 1, ... and return the first d that divides both a and b.
algorithms.pseudocode: if a = 0 or b = 0: return a + b; d = min(a, b); while d does not divide both a and b: d = d - 1; return d
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^n) iterations in the worst case: exactly min(a, b) - gcd(a, b) + 1 iterations of one or two divisions, i.e. up to 2^n - 2 on coprime n-bit inputs (>= 2^(n-2) on the coprime Fibonacci pairs used for V2: the pair is F_(k+1), F_k with F_(k+1) < 2^n <= F_(k+2), and F_(k+2) = F_(k+1) + F_k <= 3 F_k, so min(a, b) = F_k >= 2^n / 3 > 2^(n-2)). In bit operations, Theta(2^n) times the cost of an n-bit division.
algorithms.correctness: Every common divisor is at most min(a, b) (for a, b > 0), and d = 1 always divides both, so the first d found scanning downwards is the greatest common divisor.

algorithms.name: Euclid's algorithm
algorithms.idea: Replace (a, b) by (b, a mod b) until b = 0; the common divisors never change.
algorithms.pseudocode: while b != 0: (a, b) = (b, a mod b); return a
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n) division steps: at most log_phi(min(a, b)) + O(1) <= 1.44 n + O(1) (Lame 1844), attained by consecutive Fibonacci numbers. O(n^2) bit operations with schoolbook division: a step with quotient q on numbers of at most n bits costs O(n (1 + log q)), and the log q sum to at most n; Theta(n^2) on consecutive Fibonacci numbers, where each of the Theta(n) steps divides Theta(n)-bit numbers.
algorithms.correctness: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b) because a mod b = a - qb, so both pairs have the same common divisors; the second argument strictly decreases, and gcd(a, 0) = a.

relationship: Trial divisors are linear in the VALUE min(a, b), hence exponential, Theta(2^n), in the bit length n. Euclid needs only O(n) division steps (Lame) and O(n^2) bit operations: polynomial in the input size.

sources.title: The Art of Computer Programming, Vol. 2: Seminumerical Algorithms (3rd ed.)
sources.note: Section 4.5.2 (the greatest common divisor) and 4.5.3 (analysis of Euclid's algorithm, including Lame's theorem).

sources.title: Note sur la limite du nombre des divisions dans la recherche du plus grand commun diviseur entre deux nombres entiers
sources.venue: Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences (Paris) 19, 867-870
sources.note: The number of division steps is at most five times the number of decimal digits of the smaller input; consecutive Fibonacci numbers are the worst case.

verification.method: V1: both implementations agree with each other and with math.gcd (used only as the oracle) on random pairs with max(a, b) of bit length n = 0..16, 32, 64, 256, 1024 and 4096 (trial divisors up to n = 16), including pairs with a large common factor and pairs with a zero. V2 uses consecutive Fibonacci numbers, the largest pair below 2^n: they are coprime (worst case for trial divisors) and Lame's worst case for Euclid. Trial divisors fit 2^n at n = 14..22. Euclid is timed at n = 4000..64000 bits against n^2, its bit complexity: at this size every division step on CPython's multi-digit integers costs Theta(n). The O(n) step count itself is not timed: at word size (n <= 64) wall-clock time is dominated by interpreter overhead and CPython's 30-bit digit boundaries (a trial fit against n gave alpha ~1.34), so it does not isolate the step count.

caveats: Bit-size view: trial divisors are polynomial (linear) in the VALUE of the inputs and exponential only in their length. Euclid's O(n^2) bit cost assumes schoolbook division; subquadratic half-gcd algorithms (Knuth-Schonhage) reach O(M(n) log n). V2 times Euclid on numbers with thousands of bits, so it checks the bit-operation bound, not the O(n) division-step bound.
notes: Euclid's algorithm (Elements, Book VII, c. 300 B.C.) is among the oldest nontrivial algorithms still in use; Lame's 1844 bound is often cited as one of the earliest worst-case analyses of an algorithm.
